The story is a deeply original and thoughtfully crafted piece of writing that avoids cliches. Instead of relying on overused expressions or melodramatic tropes, the author uses fresh, specific, and evocative comparisons—such as describing cool skin as "the temperature of a room no one has been in all day," a raven's call as "a stick knocked against a hollow log," and an elk's bugle as "a gate opening somewhere far away." 

Furthermore, the central metaphor of the story—comparing the slow, imperceptible drift of geological survey benchmarks to the way people drift apart and the way life moves on after death—is unique and poignant. Even when the story touches on a potentially familiar cinematic trope (a spinning wheel on an overturned car), it subverts the cliche by slowing it down ("turning, very slowly, in the wind") and using it for quiet psychological reflection rather than cheap dramatic tension.
